INTRODUCTION
Congress did not intend to foreclose adjustment to
LPR status for every noncitizen whose asylum status
could be terminated.  The government agrees.  So this
case is not about why Congress would have allowed
the Attorney General to exercise discretion to grant
LPR status to refugees with criminal convictions.  All
agree he has that power.  It is about whether
Congress cut off that discretion at the moment of
termination.  Nothing in Section 1159 says that.
The absence of any express reference to the
termination of asylum, to continuing asylum status,
or to maintaining asylum at the time of examination
is powerful evidence no such condition exists.  When
Congress wanted adjustment to turn on a continuing
condition, it said so explicitly, three times in Section
1159, in those words, and in enumerated paragraphs.
The government never explains why a Congress so
careful about listing present conditions in Section
1159 would impose this one condition by implication.
The government nonetheless asks this Court to
read that implied condition into the seven words “the
status of any alien gran ted asylum.”  8 U.S.C.
§ 1159(b).  The government agrees “granted” can refer
to a completed event, and that, ultimately, it comes
down to context.  The immediate context is Section
1159, which uses “granted asylum” as a completed
event and which includes express continuing
conditions.  That “granted” or “granted asylum” refers
to a present state elsewhere carries far less weight.
The parties also agree that Section 1159
authorizes adjustment from one status to another.
The government’s only basis for limiting the former to
“asylum status” is an artifi cial parallelism it gets by

2

omitting the word “any” or rewriting it as “an[].”  And
the current status of “any” alien granted asylum need
not be asylum status to be adjusted.
The government’s absolutist reading of Section
1159 has nothing to commend it.  It would lead to the
removal of innocent spouses and children, who bear
no responsibility for triggering termination.  It would
send current refugees back to the countries from
which they fled.  And it has forced the government to
invent workarounds to prevent what all seem to agree
are untoward and unintended consequences.
No workaround is needed.  Section 1159(b) means
what it says: any noncitizen granted asylum may seek
adjustment if the five conditions Congress wrote are
satisfied.  There is no additional, implicit condition of
continuing asylum status.  And whether to adjust
remains in the Attorney General’s discretion.
ARGUMENT
“[T]he status of any alien granted asylum,” read in
context, refers to the current status of any noncitizen
who was or has been granted asylum.  Statutory
history and purpose reinforce that reading.  And any
ambiguity resolves in petitioners’ favor.
A. “Granted Asylum,” Read In Context,
Refers To A Completed Action
The government agrees “granted” is a past
participle, which may indicate completed action or
describe a present state—depending on context.
Resp. Br. 12.  But for cont ext, the government skips
over Section 1159, relying instead on a neighboring
provision and use of the wo rd “granted” elsewhere.
The immediate statutory context is more compelling.
1.  The government admits the only other use of
“granted asylum” in Section 1159 “refers to a

3

completed historical event rather than the alien’s
continuing asylum status.”  Id. a t  1 7 .   A n d  i t
acknowledges the “presumption of consistent usage.”
Id. at 16 (citation omitted).  The government
nonetheless argues that because Section 1159(b)(2)
includes an auxiliary verb and temporal language,
and the introductory clause does not, they should be
read differently.  That conclusion does not follow.
Inclusion of the phrase “at least one year after
being” in Section 1159(b)(2) makes clear the reference
is to a completed event, but the absence of comparable
language in Section 1159(b)  does not convey the
opposite.  The specific temporal language was needed
in (b)(2) to connect the grant of asylum to the one-year
time period; inserting “after being” into the
introductory language would not do the same work
and would be, at best, linguistically strained (the
status of any alien after being granted asylum).
Nor is the absence of an alternative auxiliary verb
in the introductory clause probative.  As this Court
recognized in Henson v. Santander Consumer USA
Inc., when an auxiliary verb was missing from the
statutory phrase “‘debts owed  or due … another,’” it
had to choose between auxiliary verbs:  “debts that are
owed or due another” or “debts that were owed or are
due another.”  582 U.S. 79, 81, 84 (2017) (alteration in
original) (citation omitted).  And in Florida
Department of Revenue v. Piccadilly Cafeterias, Inc. ,
this Court held the past participle in “under a plan
confirmed” indicated “past or completed action,”
despite the lack of an auxiliary verb.  554 U.S. 33,
38-39 (2008) (citations omitted).
For the phrase “granted asylum,” Congress
sometimes includes clarifying auxiliary verbs.  E.g.,
8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(4)(E)(ii) (“is granted asylum”); id.

4

§ 1613(b)(1)(B) (same); id. § 1252(e)(2)(C) (“has been
granted asylum”); id. § 1157(a)(4) (“were granted
asylum”).  And it sometimes does not.  E.g., id.
§ 1364(b)(1) (“aliens … granted asylum”);
Immigration Act of 1990, Pub. L. No. 101-649,
§ 141(c)(1)(F), 104 Stat. 4978, 5003 (1990 Act) (“aliens
granted asylum”).  So the absence just begs the
question: what auxiliary verb fits best?  Pet’rs Br.
25-26.
2. The immediate statutory context and structure
provide the answer.  Section 1159 sets forth
continuing conditions in express and enumerated
terms; it does not sneak them in through vague
introductory phrases.  And the government’s
interpretation takes away much of the Attorney
General’s discretion Section 1159(c) expressly grants.
a. Take Section 1159(a).  The introductory
language refers to “[a]ny alien who has been
admitted,” and then imposes an enumerated
condition “whose admission has not been terminated.”
8 U.S.C. § 1159(a)(1)(A).  In  the government’s view,
Congress could have said “[a]ny alien granted
admission” and it would have meant the same thing.
But that is not how Congress drafted Section 1159.
Every time Congress wanted a continuing condition,
it said so in express  terms.  It used temporal
language.  It listed the conditions in enumerated
paragraphs.  And it left no room for doubt.  See id.
§ 1159(a)(1)(A), (b)(3), (b)(5); Resp. Br. 23 (admitting
these “undoubtedly” impose continuing conditions).  If
Congress had meant “any alien who has been granted
asylum … whose asylum has not been terminated,” or
“any alien granted asylum who … continues to have
asylum,” or “any alien granted asylum who … has

5

asylum at the time of examination,” it would have
said that—and listed it as a sixth condition.
The government has three responses; none are
compelling.
First, the government says (at 24) the introductory
clause uses different la nguage because it is a
“threshold category,” rather than “an additional
condition.”  But the same is true of Section 1159(a)(1).
The parallel “threshold category” is “[a]ny alien who
has been admitted to the United States,” which is
then limited to those “whose admission has not been
terminated” in paragraph (A).  When Congress
wanted to place conditions on the “threshold
category,” it did so in the paragraphs that followed.
Second, the government argues that just because
Sections 1159(a)(1)(A), (b)(3 ), and (b)(5) are “more
obvious” does not make Section 1159(b)’s introductory
clause “less clear.”  Resp. Br. 23 (citation omitted); cf.
id. at 21 (similar).  Of course it does.  “That Congress
chose not to adopt those ‘readily available and
apparent alternative[s]’ supports the conclusion” it
did not intend to impose a continuing asylum
condition.  Mullin v. Al Otro Lado, 609 U.S. 258, 271
(2026) (alteration in original) (citation omitted); see
Advocate Health Care Network v. Stapleton, 581 U.S.
468, 477 (2017) (noting failure to adopt “ready
alternative”).
Third, the government criticizes some of
petitioners’ alternative formulations.  Resp. Br. 20-21.
But the most obvious alternatives—those used
elsewhere in Section 1159—remain untouched.
And the fact that “‘possessing’” and “‘holding’”
were not used elsewhere in the INA to refer to asylum
(at 20) does not mean Congress could not access that

6

ordinary lexicon.  Even the government inserts
“possess” to get to its interpretation.  Id. at 2-3, 24.
Plus, other comparable words, like “maintain,” were
used in similar contexts.  E.g., 8 U.S.C. §§ 1184(a)(1),
1203(b), 1251(a)(9), 1255b(a), 1258.  That included the
asylum regulation, which provided an asylum
applicant had to be “maintaining a lawful status.”
8 C.F.R. § 108.1 (1980); see 4 4  F e d .  R e g .  2 1 , 2 5 3 ,
21,256 (Apr. 10, 1979).  Congress could have readily
required applicants for adjustment to maintain, or
even just have, asylum.1
b. Section 1159(c)’s waiver authority provides
further, immediate contextual support.
The government admits “that Congress did not
intend to foreclose adjus tment to every alien whose
asylum status could be te rminated.”  Resp. Br. 35
(emphasis omitted).  It d oes not dispute that the
Attorney General’s exercise of discretion is important,
or that the grounds for termination substantially
overlap with the grounds for inadmissibility.  Pet’rs
Br. 24.  And it does not dispute that, under its
interpretation, a decision to terminate forecloses any
exercise of discretion under Section 1159(c).
The government previously sought to avoid this
problem with a workaround: IJs could simply “defer[]
ruling on a motion to terminate asylum status in favor
of first adjudicating an application for adjustment of

1  The government is right that “asylee” did not appear in
the 1980 Act or contemporaneous dictionaries, but it was not far
behind.  Congress used “asylee status” in 1981, Omnibus Budget
Reconciliation Act of 1981, Pub. L. No. 97-35, § 544(a), 95 Stat.
357, 460, and some courts referred to asylees at that time, e.g.,
Fernandez-Roque v. Smith, 539 F. Supp. 925, 932-33 (N.D. Ga.
1982); Chun v. Sava, 708 F.2d 869, 876-77 (2d Cir. 1983).

7

status.”  Pet’rs Br. 39 (citation omitted).  As
petitioners explained, that only shows Congress did
not intend a categorical bar.  So the government
proposes yet another way to reach the same result:
the IJ could choose not to terminate asylum at all.
Resp. Br. 25.  According to the government (at 36), the
IJ in Wassily’s case made that “mistake”: he never
should have terminated asylum.  That too makes
nonsense of congressional intent, and poses its own
problems.
The don’t-terminate-asylum solution does not
mean Section 1159(c) “retains its force.”  Id. at 10-11.
It would still have no work to do once asylum is
terminated.  Nor does the government’s reading
“harmonize” two “forms of discretion.”  Id. at 36.  It
simply shifts the discretion from one statutory form
(Section 1159(c)) to another (Section 1158(c)).
But the two forms of discretion are also not the
same.  Section 1159(c) is explicit about the grounds
for waiver: “humanitarian purposes, to assure family
unity, or when it is otherwise in the public interest.”
8 U.S.C. § 1159(c).  Section 1158(c)(2) just says “may.”
Id. § 1158(c)(2).  And the implementing regulation
says nothing about humanitarian, family unity, or
similar concerns; the focus for termination is whether
the noncitizen is still “eligible” for asylum.  8 C.F.R.
§ 1208.24(c); see id.  § 208.24(c).  That Wassily’s IJ
exercised the discretion granted expressly in
Section 1159(c), rather than what the government
now reimagines Section 1158(c)(2) to implicitly allow,
was no “mistake.”  It is the statutory scheme Congress
enacted.2

2  That the Attorney General “could have directed the
Board to refer [Wassily’s] case to him,” Resp. Br. 36, is no

8

The general discretion not to terminate asylum
also won’t save those most deserving of adjustment.
The government is conspicuously silent when it comes
to the innocent spouses and children granted
derivative asylum who would automatically lose the
ability to seek adjustment if the primary holder’s
asylum is terminated.  Pet’rs Br. 4, 37; see Nat’l
Immigrant Just. Ctr. Amic us Br. (NIJC Br.) 4-7;
Immigr. L. Professors Amici Br. (Profs. Br.) 16-17.
The governing regulation provides that derivative
asylum status shall terminate “automatically.”  Resp.
Br. 36; see 8 C.F.R. § 1208.24(d).  The government
never explains how the Attorney General could
terminate asylum for the principal holder but not the
derivative asylee, or wh y he would choose not to
terminate asylum for the principal without a
humanitarian, family unity, or other reason.  The
domestic-violence examples in the NIJC amicus brief
(at 7-9) put a fine point on the problem.  The
government apparently would have the Attorney
General either retain asylum status for the abuser or
terminate for all—and, in doing so, categorically
preclude the victims from seeking LPR adjustment.
Giving the Section 1159(c) waiver full force would
avoid that perverse and unnecessary tradeoff.
3. The government’s present-state interpretation
of “granted asylum,” by co ntrast, does not come from
Section 1159.  It comes from the neighboring Section
1158(c), other uses of the word “granted” in the U.S.

answer.  Self-referral is “used sparingly,” follows “no statutory
or regulatory roadmap,” and cannot be requested by immigrant
respondents.  Stella Burch Elias & Paul Gowder, Against
Attorney General Self-Referral in Immigration Law , 109 Minn.
L. Rev. 2331, 2334, 2341, 2398 (2025).

9

Code, and common usage.  None of the government’s
examples compel a present-state reading of “granted
asylum” or override the text’s statutory home.
a. Start with Section 1158(c).  As petitioners
explained, the use of “granted asylum” and “asylum
granted” there conveys a present state because of the
surrounding context.  Pet’rs Br. 26.  Section 1158(c)(2)
is all about termination of asylum, and (c)(1) requires
the Attorney General to do things that (c)(3) prohibits
him from doing when asylum is terminated.  Section
1159’s context points in the other direction.
The government attempts to link the two through
a “benefits” framing.  Resp . Br. 2, 10.  But Congress
did not.  Congress did not list adjustment to LPR
status as a benefit conferred in Section 1158.  It
provided the opportunity to seek adjustment to
refugees and asylees alike in a separate provision.
Unlike the Section 1158 benefits, which flow from the
grant of asylum itself, ad justment is a distinct,
discretionary form of relief that follows a highly
reticulated application process with numerous other
conditions a noncitizen must satisfy.
b. Zooming out further, the government (at 14)
points to examples of “granted” in the U.S. Code that
reference a present state.  But for each, the
surrounding context—not just the past participle
“granted”—suggests that reading.  A “person granted
a customs broker’s license” must “ hold[] a valid …
license” to “conduct customs business,” 19 U.S.C.
§ 1641(a)(1), (b)(1) (emphasis added); a “person
granted an exemption” may be required to
“demonstrate continued compliance” with statutory
requirements, 21 U.S.C. § 360j(m)(5) (emphasis
added); and “[p]ersons granted authority to make
arrests … may exercise that authority only while

10

guarding and protecting” certain property, 51 U.S.C.
§ 20134 (emphasis added).
And other examples point the other way.  Review
of an “allegation of misconduct by an individual
granted authority” under a statute, 2 U.S.C.
§ 185(d)(3)(E); 44 U.S.C. § 3903(c)(5), can occur
whether or not the individual still possesses that
authority.  Receiving “reimbursement” from a “person
granted [an] exemption,” 15 U.S.C. § 2603(c)(3)(A),
can happen even if the exemption has since lapsed.
Other uses of “granted asylum” in the U.S. Code,
though also not uniform, are more to the point.
Several “granted asylum” provisions include express
temporal language to require continuing asylum
status.  E.g., 8 U.S.C. § 1252(e)(2)(C) (“petitioner …
has been granted asylum under section 1158 of this
title, such status not having been terminated ”
(emphasis added)); id. § 1641(b)(2) (“‘qualified alien’
means an alien who, at the time the alien applies for,
receives, or attempts to receive a Federal public
benefit, is … an alien who is  granted asylum”
(emphases added)).  That  Congress followed this
approach for the continuing conditions in Section
1159 itself, but not for “granted asylum,” is more
probative than disparate uses of “granted” elsewhere.
c. The government’s “common-usage examples”
(at 14-15) fare no better.  Once again, there are
counter-examples.  If a company provided that any
employee granted a security clearance must keep all
information confidential, no one would think the
employee could hold a press conference if his security
clearance was revoked.  And a person granted
coverage under an insurance policy may still submit
a claim after the policy expires or is terminated.

11

The bigger problem is the government’s examples
fail to track Section 1159.  They assume a guaranteed
benefit where only an opportunity to apply exists.  So
the closer analogy would be if any person granted an
honorary degree may request a seat at a celebratory
dinner (subject to the university president’s
discretion).  Or if a lawy er admitted to the Supreme
Court Bar may request a seat in the bar section
(subject to the Chief Justice’s discretion).  The
government’s examples also assume readers will infer
a continuing condition based  on context and when it
seems absurd not to.  But Section 1159 takes a
different approach: it includes express continuing
conditions.  And granting the Attorney General
discretion to adjust a former asylee’s status (including
a former derivative asylee’s status) to LPR status in
appropriate circumstances is far from absurd.
B. The Attorney General Can Adjust The
Current Status Of A Noncitizen
Previously Granted Asylum
The government’s other textual hook is the word
“status.”  It argues (i) “status” denotes a present
condition; (ii) Section 1159(b) authorizes “an
adjustment from one status to the other”; and (iii) the
“parallel structure” and “parallel language” show the
pre-adjustment status must  be “asylum status.”
Resp. Br. 12-13, 22.  The first and second are true, but
the third does not follow.  There is no parallel.
1. The parties agree that “status” denotes a
present condition.  Pet’rs Br. 19-20; Resp. Br. 22.  The
parties also agree the Attorney General is adjusting
from one status to another.  Pet’rs Br. 19-20; Resp.
Br. 13.  And although both the Second and Fourth
Circuits seemed to believe “status” can only be a

12

“legal” status, Pet. App. 12a; Cela v. Garland , 75
F.4th 355, 364 (4th Cir. 2023) , the government does
not defend that position.  For good reason: it is
demonstrably wrong.  See Pet’rs Br. 19-20; Am.
Immigr. Lawyers Ass’n Amicus Br. 16-18.
2. The only question, then , is whether the phrase
“the status of any alien granted asylum” refers to
“asylum status” only or to any “status” the noncitizen
currently holds.  The government argues the former
based on Section 1159(b)’s  “parallel” structure and
language.  But it elides one critical flaw: the two
clauses are not, in fact, parallel.
Congress wrote “ an alien lawfully admitted for
permanent residence” but “ any alien granted
asylum.”  The government has to rewrite the second
phrase as “an[] alien gran ted asylum” to make them
match.  Resp. Br. 13.  And it repeatedly does exactly
that, truncating the statutory phrase to “alien
granted asylum,” e.g., id. at 2, 10, 15, 23, or altering
it to “an[] alien granted asylum,” id. at 3, 13, to create
artificial parallelism.  No matter how many times the
government does so, the statute says what it says.
The government dismisses the inconvenient word
“any” as too “oblique” to matter.  Id. at 22.  And it
points to a 1997 Senate dr afting manual to explain
away its significance.  Id.  But that source supports
petitioners’ reading.  As the manual instructs, while
the indefinite article “an” should “[g]enerally” be
used, “any” should be used instead “[i]f there is any
possibility that a provision could be read to apply to
fewer than all of the member s of the class.”  Office
of the Legislative Counsel, U.S. Senate, Legislative
Drafting Manual  § 104(b)(1)-(2) (1997),
https://law.yale.edu/sites/default/files/documents/pdf/
Faculty/SenateOfficeoftheLegislativeCounsel_Legisl

13

ativeDraftingManual%281997%29.pdf.  Who could
Congress have been concerned about excluding other
than noncitizens whose asylum was later terminated?
Because Congress chose to use “any” (when “an alien
granted asylum” would have worked perfectly well
grammatically), the full class is included.  See Bernal
v. NRA Grp., LLC , 930 F.3d 891, 896 (7th Cir. 2019)
(“absent limiting language, ‘any’ should mean ‘any’”).
Nor would a quasi-parallel structure carry the day
regardless.  The first general adjustment provision
used similar language and a similar (albeit inverted)
structure:
The status of an alien who was lawfully
admitted to the United States as a bona
fide nonimmigrant and who is
continuing to maintain that status  may
be adjusted by the Attorney General in
his discretion … to that of an alien
lawfully admitted for permanent
residence ….
Immigration and Nationality Act, Pub. L. No. 82-414,
§ 245(a), 66 Stat. 163, 217 ( 1952) (emphasis added).
It permitted the Attorney General to adjust from one
status (“[t]he status of an alien who was lawfully
admitted to the United States as a bona fide
nonimmigrant”) to another (the status of “an alien
lawfully admitted for permanent residence”).  Id.  But
there is no question the 1958 version of this statutory
provision did not require continuing status.  Congress
intentionally deleted the phrase “who is continuing to
maintain that status” an d left the grammatical
structure intact.  Pet’rs Br. 27-28.
3. The government’s other arguments are
unavailing.

14

The government claims that provisions letting
noncitizens without lawful  status adjust “look
nothing like” Section 1159(b)  because they expressly
name an unlawful starting status.  Resp. Br. 22.  That
misses the point.  Those provisions show what the
courts of appeals got wrong, and what the government
does not dispute: that unlawful status is still a
“status” from which a noncitizen can adjust.  Pet’rs
Br. 20.  They also each  mention unlawful status
because they are limited to that status.  See 8 U.S.C.
§§ 1255(c)(2), 1255b(a), 1229b(b )(1).  Section 1159(b)
is not.  And when Congress means to exclude unlawful
status, it says so.  E.g., id. § 1255(c)(2).
The government next says Congress “manifestly
knows how to provide aliens with immigration
benefits that are not conditioned on present status,”
highlighting 8 U.S.C. § 1158(a)(1) and 8 U.S.C.
§ 1255(a).  Resp. Br. 13-14.  But Section 1255(a) looks
just like Section 1159(b): it gives the Attorney
General discretion to adjust “[t]he status of an alien
who was inspected and admitted or paroled into the
United States” into that “of an alien lawfully admitted
for permanent residence.”  The only difference is
Section 1255(a) identifies “threshold eligibility,”
Resp. Br. 14, as those “inspected and admitted or
paroled into the United States,” and Section 1159(b)
identifies it as those “g ranted asylum.”  Neither
dictates what the starting “status” needs to be.  And
adding “irrespective of such  alien’s status,” 8 U.S.C.
§ 1158(a)(1), to Section 1159(b) would at best be
superfluous and at worst be inaccurate—after all, the
noncitizen must “continue[] to be a refugee,” id.
§ 1159(b)(3).
By contrast, Congress manifestly does know how
to say the opposite: that eligibility is conditioned on a

15

specific, present status.  Section 1255a refers to
temporary residents “suc h status not having
changed,” id. § 1255a(h)(3)(A)(iii); cf. id. § 1101(a)(20)
(same, for “lawfully admitted for permanent
residence”); Section 1252(e )(2)(C) asks whether a
noncitizen “has been granted asylum … such status
not having been terminated,” id. § 1252(e)(2)(C); and
a litany of provisions require that the noncitizen
“maintain” a specific “status,” see supra  at 6.  If
termination of asylum status were a bar, or
maintenance of such status  a requirement, Congress
would have said that.
In the end, “any alien granted asylum” simply
describes a “category of eligible aliens.”  Resp. Br. 24.
And “the status of” natura lly refers to whatever
status the members of that category currently hold.
C. The Statutory History Reinforces That
Contextual Reading
1. The government does not contest the history of
the general adjustment prov ision, 8 U.S.C. § 1255.
Resp. Br. 30; see Pet’rs Br. 27-28, 30-31.  It argues
that history does not prove “Congress uses only a
limited set of phrases to  convey a continuing
requirement.”  Resp. Br. 30.   The point is not that
Congress has a limited vocabulary.  It is that the
phrasing Congress used in Section 1159(b)—“any
alien granted asylum”—differs in kind from that
historical precedent and from the Section 1159
provisions setting forth continuing conditions.  See
supra a t  4 - 6 .   A n d  w h i l e  t h e  g o v e r n m e n t  d e e m s  i t
“exceedingly unlikely” the 1980 Congress had the
1952 statute in mind, there are reasons to think
otherwise.  E.g., H.R. Rep. No. 96-608, at 2-5 (1979)

16

(referring to the “origin quotas of the 1952
immigration law”).
2. The government also seeks to marginalize the
statutory history of Sections 1158 and 1159.
As explained, the 1980 Act contained a single
ground for terminating refugee status and a single
ground for terminating asylum status; the
adjustment provision tracked the termination
provision; and Section 1159(b) dealt with criminal
conduct through admissibility and waiver.  Pet’rs Br.
29-30.  In 1996, Congress expanded the statutory
grounds for terminating asylum, but it did not change
the language in Section 1159(b)’s introductory clause.
Id. at 31-32.  From that, petitioners argued, in 1980,
“a continuing asylum status requirement would have
done no work and served no purpose.”  Id. at 30.  The
government says that is  “incorrect” (at 31) and
identifies three purposes.  The first two rely on
regulatory provisions that postdate and conflict with
the statute, and the third is makeweight.
First, the government notes that a regulation
adopted to “implement[]” Section 1158 allowed for
termination based on “‘conviction of a serious crime.’”
Resp. Br. 34 (quoting 8 C.F. R. § 208.15(a)(2) (1981)).
But as the government sheepishly acknowledges, that
regulation may not have been “consistent with the
statutory language.”  Id.  It was not:  The 1980 Act
provided a single ground for terminating asylum,
with limited authority to make a “determin[ation]
that the alien is no longer a refugee” “pursuant to”
prescribed regulations.  Pu b. L. No. 96-212, § 201(b),
94 Stat. 102, 105 (1980) (addi ng § 208(b)).  So the
conclusion stands: under the 1980 Act, noncitizens
with criminal convictions would not have been

17

categorically barred from adjusting to LPR status.
Pet’rs Br. 30.
Second, the government relies on the same
“implementing” regulation to argue that asylum could
be terminated if the asylee was not “eligible for
asylum when it was granted.”  Resp. Br. 32 (citing
8 C.F.R. § 208.15(a)(3) (1981)).   That too appears at
odds with the statute.  And perhaps more to the point,
the 1980 Congress chose to address potential fraud in
another way—the same way it addressed criminal
convictions—through inadmissibility.  At that time,
the inadmissibility statute provided that “seek[ing] to
procure … a visa or other documentation, or seek[ing]
to enter the United States[]  by fraud or by willfully
misrepresenting a material fact,” was grounds to “be
excluded from admission in to the United States.”
8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(19) (1982) .  So a noncitizen who
committed fraud in applying for asylum would not
have been “admissible … at the time of examination
for adjustment” under Section 1159(b)(5), but would
have been eligible for a Section 1159(c) waiver.
Third, the government says a continuing asylum
requirement would have allowed it to avoid
answering the continuing refugee question twice—
first to terminate asylum, and then to bar adjustment
under (b)(3).  Resp. Br. 31.  That concern appears to
be hypothetical at best—especially because, in
practice, the two decisions are often made at roughly
the same time.  There is no reason to think Congress
adopted a categorical bar that would do so little work.
The government’s other arguments are
nonresponsive.  It cont ends Section 1159(b)(3) was
not superfluous (at 33), but superfluity was never
petitioners’ argument.  It argues that Congress did
not need to add any “additional words” to Section

18

1159(b) in 1996 because current asylum status was
already a “threshold condition.”  Id. at 33-34.  But that
assumes the conclusion.  The better understanding is
the 1980 Congress did not include a continuing
asylum requirement because it did not need a
continuing asylum requirement—and Section 1159(b)
looks the same today as it did then.
3.  The government relies heavily on the statutory
note added by the 1990 Act.   As the government
concedes, that Act was meant to solve a specific
problem facing noncitizens who no longer qualified as
refugees following the Cold War.  Id. at 25-26.  The
government nevertheless contends the Act
“operate[d] on the assumption” that only current
asylees could adjust under Section 1159(b).  Id. at
17-19, 25-29.  The only text the government points to
cannot bear the weight the government places on it.
The first “provision” (at 18) the government cites
is, in fact, just a title.  The government reads the title
of Section 104(c), “Waiver of Numerical Limitation for
Certain Current Asylees,” to mean that Congress
considered only current asylees to be valid applicants
for adjustment.  Id. at 18-19.  But Section 104(c) also
waives the numerical limitation for “an alien
described in subsection (d),” that is, former asylees.
1990 Act, Pub. L. No. 101- 649, § 104(c)-(d), 104 Stat.
4978, 4985.  A “Current Asyl ees” title for a statutory
provision that expressly co vers former asylees just
underscores why a title “cannot substitute for the
operative text of the statute.”  Piccadilly Cafeterias,
Inc., 554 U.S. at 47.
The second provision is Section 104(d).  Petitioners
already addressed the parenthetical (at 34-35), and
the government accepts it  served a “clarifying”
purpose—at least as to Section 104(d)(1)(A), Resp. Br.

19

27.  But the bright line the government seeks to draw
between “the phrasing of  Section 104(d)(1)(A)” and
“Section 1159(b) itself,” id., does not hold up.  The only
difference between them is the addition of the
auxiliary verb “was.”  Co ngress needed to include
“was” in Section 104(d)(1)(A) because it keys the grant
of asylum to a particular date.  Section 1159(b) does
not.  And while Section 1159(b) does not say “was,” it
also does not say the opposite.  The question is what
auxiliary verb (or other word s) to read in.  Section
104(d)(1)(A) does not answer that question, and the
government agrees the parenthetical is clarifying if
the answer is “was.”
Section 104(d)(1)(C) points to petitioners’ reading.
It provides for adjustment if a noncitizen “was (or
would be) qualified … but for paragraphs (2) and (3)”
of Section 1159(b).  1990 Act § 104(d)(1)(C), 104 Stat.
at 4985-86.  If the 1990 Act operated on the
assumption that continuing asylum status was a
condition for adjustment under Section 1159(b)’s
introductory clause, it would have excepted that
condition too.  That it did not is at least as indicative
of Congress’s understanding as (A)’s parenthetical.
The legislative history the government cites is not
to the contrary.  As the government notes, the
statement was about an unenacted, proposed
amendment that would have eliminated the
“continues to be a refugee” requirement.  Resp. Br. 27.
That history does not reveal the basis for that one
Representative’s view; whet her others shared it; or
whether the concerns were deemed unfounded.  It
instead exemplifies why “failed legislative
proposals”—or, worse, legislative history about failed
legislative proposals—“are ‘a particularly dangerous
ground on which to rest an interpretation of a prior

20

statute.’”  United States v. Craft , 535 U.S. 274, 287
(2002) (citation omitted); see United States v. Estate of
Romani, 523 U.S. 517, 536 (1998) (Scalia, J.,
concurring in part and concurring in the judgment).
Finally, congressional intent a decade later cannot
shed meaningful light on the 1980 Act.  The
government argues otherwise based on Watson v.
Republican National Committee, 609 U.S. 672 (2026).
But Watson stands for a more limited proposition: a
later-enacted statute can inform the interpretation of
an earlier, ambiguous statute when the two are “at
odds with” each other and the later statute otherwise
would “make little sense.”  Id. at 684, 690.  That’s not
this case.  The 1980 Act an d the 1990 statutory note
are not “at odds” under either interpretation, and the
latter is fully operative under petitioners’.  This is
instead a situation where a statute “enacted” a decade
“after the fact” should not be “probative of th[e]
meaning” of the earlier-enacted statute “at the time it
became law.”  Id. at 711 (Alito, J. , dissenting); see
O’Gilvie v. United States, 519 U.S. 79, 89-90 (1996).3
D.  The Government’s Reading Does Nothing
To Further Congressional Purpose
The government has nothing affirmative to say
about Congress’s purposes.  It never once argues that

3  Contrary to the government’s assertion (at 29), the “tax
year” had nothing to do with why O’Gilvie “declined to rely on” a
later amendment to interpret the original statute.  The
argument was that Congress would not have enacted the later
provision (removing punitive damages in nonphysical injury
cases) unless it believed the existing law included punitive
damages.  519 U.S. at 88-89.  And Bostock v. Clayton County, 590
U.S. 644, 670 (2020), was also about other “enacted” statutes, not
just congressional inaction.  Contra Resp. Br. 29.

21

petitioners’ reading contravenes any such purpose,
focusing instead on why its reading doesn’t either.
As petitioners argued (at 35-38) and amici
explained (NIJC Br. 4-25; Profs. Br. 16-19), Congress
had many reasons to let th e Attorney General adjust
the status of refugees whose asylum had been
terminated.  The government agrees—with one twist.
It acknowledges that noncitizens can lose asylum for
reasons outside their control, or for relatively minor
crimes, and that there may be other “sympathetic
circumstances.”  Resp. Br. 35-38.  It just says the
Attorney General’s discretion must be exercised
before termination.  That’s no answer for reasons
already explained.  See supra at 6-8.  And if the end
result is the same, why did Congress draw such a
bright temporal line in such an oblique way?  The
government does not say.
And while the government notes that refugees and
asylees are treated differently in some respects (at
37), it does not explain why they would be treated
differently in this respect.  Take a refugee and an
asylee with the same conviction.  The refugee may
seek adjustment and a waiver; under the
government’s reading, the asylee (who still fears
persecution) may not.  That asymmetry defies
Congress’s plan to give asylees a status “equivalent in
most respects” to refugees.  S. Rep. No. 96-256, at 9
(1979), reprinted in 1980 U.S.C.C.A.N. 141, 149; see
Robleto-Pastora v. Holder , 591 F.3d 1051, 1061 (9th
Cir. 2010).
E. Any Ambiguity Favors Petitioners
The government would confine the immigration
rule of lenity to “deportation statute[s].”  Resp. Br. 38-
40.  But it cites no case imposing that limit.  Nor can

22

such a limit be squared with the rule’s rationale:
because deportation is “a drastic measure,” the Court
“will not assume that Congress meant to trench on [a
noncitizen’s] freedom beyond that which is required
by the narrowest of the seve ral possible meanings.”
Id. at 38 (alteration in original) (quoting Fong Haw
Tan v. Phelan, 333 U.S. 6, 10 (1948)).  That rationale
turns on the result of the interpretation, not the
provision’s label.
The government does not dispute that INS v.
Errico, 385 U.S. 214 (1966), INS v. St. Cyr , 533 U.S.
289 (2001), and Dada v. Mukasey, 554 U.S. 1 (2008),
applied lenity to relief provisions that were not
“deportation statutes.”  It argues only that they were
more “directly connected” to removal.  Resp. Br. 39.
But that’s a different line than “deportation statutes.”
And they were no closer to  removal than this one.
Pet’rs Br. 43; Profs. Br . 15-16, 20-22.  Indeed, INS v.
Cardoza-Fonseca, 480 U.S. 421, 449-50 (1987),
construed the asylum standard itself.  And the
government does not disput e that once asylum is
terminated, removal follows.  Pet’rs Br. 42.
The government’s only contrary authorities—
Swan & Finch Co. v. United States , 190 U.S. 143
(1903), and United States v. Manzi , 276 U.S. 463
(1928)—predate Fong Haw Tan  and did not involve
removal.  Resp. Br. 38-39.  Swan concerned a
commercial customs privilege, 190 U.S. at 145-46,
while Manzi concerned citizenship, a “high privilege,”
276 U.S. at 467.
Finally, the government would require “grievous”
ambiguity to invoke lenity.  Resp. Br. 40 (quoting
Pugin v. Garland , 599 U.S. 600, 610 (2023)).  Pugin
adopted no such threshold; it found the statute clear.
599 U.S. at 610.  And this Court has applied

23

immigration lenity to “lingering ambiguities,”
Cardoza-Fonseca, 480 U.S. at 449; St. Cyr, 533 U.S.
at 320, and where there was “some doubt,” Errico, 385
U.S. at 225.  Even in criminal cases, the “grievous”
formulation lacks a settled pedigree.  See Wooden v.
United States, 595 U.S. 360, 392- 93 (2022) (Gorsuch,
J., concurring in the judgment); Moskal v. United
States, 498 U.S. 103, 108 (1990) (asking whether
“reasonable doubt persists”).
Regardless, if there is ambiguity here, it is
grievous: the circuits are divided, the judges on both
the Second and Fourth Circuit panels were divided,
and the BIA found Section 1159(b) ambiguous.
Matter of T-C-A- , 28 I. & N. Dec. 472, 475-76 (B.I.A.
2022).  Any ambiguity should be construed in
petitioners’ favor.
CONCLUSION
The judgments of the court of appeals should be
reversed.
